First Chapter: Suvīra Sutta [The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? "The person who is like a well-bred horse; the person who is like a thoroughbred elephant; the person who is like a lion; and the person who is like a bull. "And how, monks, is one a person like a well-bred horse? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. "He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. "He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. "He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. "This, monks, is how one is a person like a well-bred horse. "And how, monks, is one a person like a thoroughbred elephant? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dhamma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... "This, monks, is how one is a person like a thoroughbred elephant. "And how, monks, is one a person like a lion? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dhamma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... "This, monks, is how one is a person like a lion. "And how, monks, is one a person like a bull? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... unwavering confidence in the Dhamma... unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... "This, monks, is how one is a person like a bull. "These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: "Just as a well-bred horse, Endowed with the marks of a thoroughbred, Is swift, strong, and capable, So too is the disciple of the Buddha. "Just as a thoroughbred elephant, Trained by a skilled mahout, Bears the burden of the king, So too is the disciple of the Buddha. "Just as a lion, the king of beasts, Roams the mountain caves, Fearless and undaunted, So too is the disciple of the Buddha. "Just as a bull, the leader of the herd, Roars amidst the cattle, Mighty and unshakable, So too is the disciple of the Buddha. "Monks, these are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. [End of] Suvīra Sutta, the First in the First Chapter.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Once upon a time, monks, the asuras marched against the devas.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Suvīra:
‘Dear Suvīra, these asuras are marching against the devas.’”
“Go, dear Suvīra, and counter-attack the asuras!
“Very well, venerable sir,” the deva-son Suvīra replied to Sakka, lord of the devas, yet he fell into negligence.
A second time, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the deva-son Suvīra:
‘These Asuras, dear Suvīra, are attacking the devas.
Go, dear Suvīra, and counter-attack the Asuras.
‘Very well, venerable sir,’ the deva-son Suvīra replied to Sakka, lord of the devas, yet for a second time he fell into negligence.
For a third time, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the deva-son Suvīra:
“Dear Suvīra, these asuras are attacking the devas.
Go, dear Suvīra, and counter-attack the asuras!”
“‘So be it, venerable sir,’ Suvīra the deva-son replied to Sakka, lord of the devas, and for a third time he fell into negligence.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed Suvīra the deva-son with a verse:
‘Without exertion, without striving, ...’”
“Where one attains happiness,
O valiant one, go there; and cause me to reach that very place.”
‘Alas, he does not rise up,
nor does he perform his duties; though he has all his desires fulfilled, [he is like a tree with fruit that no one eats].’
"Grant me that boon, O Sakka.
"Where the indolent man who does not exert himself attains ultimate happiness— "
“Suvīra, go there and cause me to reach that very place. “Not by action,
O best of gods,” [he replied].
“O Sakka, may we find that happiness which is free from sorrow and free from distress;
O Sakka, point out that boon to me.”
“If there were anyone anywhere who lived by non-action,
that indeed would be the path to Nibbāna.”
"Go there, Suvīra, and bring Mañca back to that very place.

Monks, even Sakka, lord of the devas, while living off the fruit of his own merit and exercising sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the Tāvatiṃsa devas, will be one who speaks in praise of initiative and energy.
“Monks, it would indeed be fitting for you that, having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline,
you should exert yourselves, strive, and endeavor for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the direct experience of the as-yet-unexperienced.”

At Sāvatthī,
the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Once upon a time, bhikkhus, the asuras marched against the devas.”
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Susīma:
“Dear Susīma, these asuras are attacking the devas.
Go, dear Susīma, and counter-attack the asuras!”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the young deva Susīma replied to Sakka, lord of the devas, and he fell into negligence.
A second time, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Susīma...
[and so on] ...a second time he fell into negligence.
A third time, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Susīma...
[as before] ...and a third time he fell into negligence.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the young deva Susīma with a verse:
“Without exertion and without striving,
where one finds happiness—
go there, Susīma.”
‘And cause him to fall right there.
‘He does not rise for his elders, nor does he perform his duties;’
“O Sakka, grant me this boon: that for one whose every desire is fulfilled, wherever he is indolent and makes no effort,” so he said.
“Wherever one is indolent and makes no effort...”
“He attains ultimate happiness;
Susīma, go there and cause me to reach that very place.”
"O Sakka, best of gods, may we find through merit that happiness which is free from sorrow and free from distress."
"Grant me this boon, Sakka!
"If there is anyone anywhere who does not live by means of action," [he replied].
"For that is the path to Nibbāna;
Susīma, go there, and cause me to reach that very place."
For indeed, monks, even Sakka, lord of the devas, while living off the fruit of his own merit and exercising sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the Tāvatiṃsa devas,
will be one who speaks in praise of initiative and energy. How much more, monks, would it befit you, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya,
to exert yourselves, to strive, and to endeavor for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the reaching of the unreached!
“...for the realization of that which has not yet been realized.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 11.3 (SN 11.3, SN 249, PTS [1st ed. SN i 218, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 472) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Once upon a time, monks, a battle had been arrayed between the devas and the asuras.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
‘If, dear sirs, fear, trepidation, or horripilation should arise in the devas when they have entered the battle, you should at that time look up at the top of my banner.’”
For as you look up at my crest, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
If you do not look up at my crest, then you should look up at the crest of Pajāpati, the king of the gods.
For as you look up at the crest of Pajāpati, the king of the gods, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
If you do not look at the crest of the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the gods, then you should look at the crest of the banner of Varuṇa, the king of the gods.
For as you look at the crest of the banner of Varuṇa, the king of the gods, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
If you do not look at the crest of the banner of Varuṇa, the king of the gods, then you should look at the crest of the banner of Īsāna, the king of the gods.
‘For as you gaze upon the crest of the banner of Īsāna, the king of the gods, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
And furthermore, monks, that same thing occurs for those who gaze upon the crest of the banner of Sakka, the lord of the devas;
or those who gaze upon the crest of the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the gods; or those who gaze upon the crest of the banner of Varuṇa, the king of the gods.
For those looking up at the crest of the banner of Īsāna, the king of the gods, whatever fear, trepidation,
or horripilation may arise, it might be abandoned, or it might not be abandoned. For what reason?
“Bhikkhus, Sakka, the lord of the devas, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion; he is fearful, timid, terrified, and prone to flight.
But I, bhikkhus, say this to you:

‘If, bhikkhus, while you have gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, fear or timidity or horripilation should arise in you, then at that time you should recollect me thus:’”

“Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
For you, monks, as you recollect me, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
If you do not recollect me, then you should recollect the Dhamma:
“The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
For as you recollect the Dhamma, monks, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
If you do not recollect the Dhamma, then you should recollect the Saṅgha:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced methodically;
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced appropriately—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals.
This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of reverential salutation.”
“The unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
For, bhikkhus, as you recollect the Saṅgha, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned. Why is that?
“For the Tathāgata, bhikkhus—worthy and perfectly enlightened—is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion; he is fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and does not flee.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“O monks, in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut,
you should recollect the Fully Enlightened One.”
There shall be no fear for you.
Should you not remember the Buddha,
the eldest in the world, the bull among men;
Then you should remember the Dhamma,
which leads to liberation and has been well-expounded.
If you do not remember the Dhamma, [you will fall away].
It leads to liberation and is well-expounded;
therefore, you should remember the Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
Thus for those who remember the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, O bhikkhus,
fear or trepidation—
“There will be no bristling of the hair,” [he said].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 11.4 (SN 11.4, SN 250, PTS [1st ed. SN i 220; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 475) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
The Discourse to Vepacitti.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Once upon a time, monks, a battle had been joined between the gods and the asuras."
Then, monks, Vepacitti the lord of the asuras addressed the asuras: “Friends, if,
when the gods and asuras have drawn up their battle lines for combat, the asuras should conquer and the gods should be defeated,
you should bind Sakka, the lord of the gods, with bonds that include his neck, and bring him into my presence at Asurapura.”
Sakka too, monks, the lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas: "If, sirs,
when the devas and asuras have drawn up their battle lines, the devas should win and the asuras should be defeated,
then you should bind Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, with bonds that include his neck as the fifth, and bring him before me to the Sudhamma assembly hall."
In that battle, monks, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.

Then, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas bound Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, with five bonds including his neck, and brought him into the presence of Sakka, lord of the devas, into the Sudhamma assembly hall.
There, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, being bound by five bonds including his neck, [stood before] Sakka...
As Sakka, lord of the devas, was entering and leaving the Sudhamma assembly hall, [a certain being] reviled and abused him with improper and harsh words.
Then, monks, Mātali the charioteer addressed Sakka, lord of the devas, in verses:
“Is it out of fear, O Maghavan Sakka,
or out of weakness that you endure hearing harsh words?”
‘Face to face with Vepacitti. [He replied:
‘It is not out of fear, nor out of weakness, that I forgive Vepacitti;’
"How indeed could one like me, who is wise,
engage in conflict with a fool?
"Only the fools would become even more divided."
And there would be no one to restrain him;
therefore, with a severe punishment,
the wise man should restrain the fool.
"I consider this alone to be the restraint of a fool:
knowing that another is provoked to anger,"
‘He who approaches one who is mindful’—
this alone, Vāsava, I see as a fault in forbearance.
When the fool thinks,
"He endures this out of fear of me," that dull-witted one climbs upon him.
‘They flee even more than cows.
Whether he thinks so or not,
this [ascetic] endures out of fear.
The highest good among all things is one's own welfare;
there is nothing found superior to patience.
For he who, though being powerful, remains—
The weak person endures [insults];
they say that is the supreme patience,
for the weak person always forgives.
They say that strength is no strength at all for one whose strength is the strength of a fool;
but for the strong man protected by the Dhamma, it is true strength.
There is no retaliation that exists [equal to it].
He who returns anger for anger is made worse off by that very act.
By not retaliating against one who is angry,
one wins a battle difficult to win;
he acts for the benefit of both.
Both for oneself and for another:
he who, knowing another is provoked,
remains composed and mindful.
While both are seeking healing—
for themselves and for another—
people think, "He is a fool."
“Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma.

For even Sakka, bhikkhus, lord of the devas, while living off the fruit of his own merit and exercising sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the Tāvatiṃsa devas, would be one who speaks in praise of patience and gentleness.
But it would be fitting for you, bhikkhus, that having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, you yourselves should be patient and gentle.

"Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of victory. What two? The victory of well-spoken words and the victory of weapons. Of these two, bhikkhus, the victory of well-spoken words is superior to the victory of weapons. "Bhikkhus, when one has won the victory of well-spoken words, one does not seek the victory of weapons. When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not gain fame; rather, one becomes ill-famed, of bad reputation, and one’s name is not spread abroad. “Bhikkhus, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they gain fame; they become well-famed, of good reputation, and their name is spread abroad. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one gains fame; one becomes well-famed, of good reputation, and one’s name is spread abroad. “Bhikkhus, when a person is poor in these five ways, they do not attain greatness; rather, they remain small, lowly, and insignificant. What five? When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not attain greatness; rather, one remains small, lowly, and insignificant. “Bhikkhus, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they attain greatness; they become great, eminent, and distinguished. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one attains greatness; one becomes great, eminent, and distinguished. “Bhikkhus, when a person is poor in these five ways, they do not cross over the flood; rather, they are swept away by the flood. What five? When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not cross over the flood; rather, one is swept away by the flood. “Bhikkhus, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they cross over the flood; they are not swept away by the flood. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one crosses over the flood; one is not swept away by the flood. “Bhikkhus, when a person is poor in these five ways, they do not reach the further shore; rather, they remain on this shore. What five? When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not reach the further shore; rather, one remains on this shore. “Bhikkhus, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they reach the further shore; they go beyond to the further shore. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one reaches the further shore; one goes beyond to the further shore. “Bhikkhus, when a person is poor in these five ways, they do not transcend birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, they do not transcend suffering, I say. What five? When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not transcend birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, one does not transcend suffering, I say. “Bhikkhus, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they transcend birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, they transcend suffering, I say. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one transcends birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, one transcends suffering, I say. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the bhikkhus considered: “Friends, the Blessed One taught us the discourse on the five kinds of poverty and the five kinds of wealth.

Now, what is the meaning of this? Then the Venerable Ānanda approached those bhikkhus and, having approached, he said to them: “Friends, why have you gathered here? “Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One taught us the discourse on the five kinds of poverty and the five kinds of wealth. Now, what is the meaning of this? “Friends, it is as if one were to throw a yoke with a single hole onto a great mountain range. It would be difficult to find a second hole to fit it through. Even so, friends, it is rare for a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One to appear in the world. It is rare to hear a Dhamma talk from the presence of a Tathāgata. And yet, friends, the Blessed One has taught us this discourse on the five kinds of poverty and the five kinds of wealth. Come, friends, let us approach the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it. “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, just now, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the bhikkhus considered: ‘Friends, the Blessed One taught us the discourse on the five kinds of poverty and the five kinds of wealth. Now, what is the meaning of this? Then the Venerable Ānanda approached those bhikkhus... [as above] ...and asked the Blessed One about the meaning of this. Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this? “Ānanda, when a person is poor in these five ways, they do not gain fame; rather, they become ill-famed, of bad reputation, and their name is not spread abroad. What five? When one is poor in faith, poor in virtue, poor in learning, poor in generosity, and poor in wisdom, one does not gain fame; rather, one becomes ill-famed, of bad reputation, and one’s name is not spread abroad. This, Ānanda, is the meaning of that statement. [The Blessed One then repeated the entire discourse in full, word for word, as previously spoken. “Ānanda, when a person is wealthy in these five ways, they transcend birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, they transcend suffering, I say. What five? When one is wealthy in faith, wealthy in virtue, wealthy in learning, wealthy in generosity, and wealthy in wisdom, one transcends birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; rather, one transcends suffering, I say. This, Ānanda, is the meaning of that statement. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.14: The Discourse on Poverty (Daliddasutta
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a certain man in this very Rājagaha was poor, destitute, and wretched among men.”
Thus, he undertook faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata; he undertook virtue; he undertook learning; he undertook generosity; he undertook wisdom.

Having undertaken faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, with the breakup of the body, after death, he [was reborn] in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
He was reborn into the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
There he outshone the other devas both in beauty and in glory.
Then, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas were indignant, disparaging, and resentful, saying:
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
For this son of the gods, when he was formerly a human being, was poor among humans, wretched among humans, and miserable among humans;
yet, with the breakup of the body, after death, he has been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.’
Thus he outshines the other gods both in beauty and in glory.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
‘Do not, sirs, find fault with this son of the devas.’
"Friends, this son of the gods, having previously been a human being, undertook faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata; he undertook virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Having undertaken faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
"He has been reborn in companionship with the gods of the Thirty-three,
and he outshines the other gods both in beauty and in glory.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the gods, addressing the gods of the Thirty-three, on that occasion recited these verses:
“He who has faith unshakable, well-established in the Tathāgata,
and whose virtue is noble— ”
Beloved by the Noble Ones and praised.
Whoever has confidence in the Saṅgha and whose vision is upright;
They say that for such a person life is not in vain;
therefore, faith and virtue—
“Faith and the vision of the Dhamma—
let the wise person devote themselves to these,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.15 (SN 11.15, SN 261, PTS [1st ed. SN i 232, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 499) 2. Second Chapter: On Delightful Places (Rāmaṇeyyakavagga) The Discourse on Delightful Places (Rāmaṇeyyakasutta) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four delightful places. What four? A delightful place where one has never before dwelt; a delightful place where one has dwelt before; a delightful place where one has seen a holy person; and a delightful place where one has heard that a holy person has dwelt. These, monks, are the four delightful places.”
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove.

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the delight of the earth?”
“Monastery shrines, forest shrines,
well-constructed lotus ponds,
and delightful human groves— ”
They are not worth a sixteenth part of it—
whether in the village or in the forest,
whether in the lowlands or on the high ground.
“Wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.16 (SN 11.16, SN 262, PTS [1st ed. SN i 233; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 500)*
2. The Second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Sacrificer.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“For those people who are making offerings...”
For living beings seeking merit who perform worldly meritorious deeds,
where is a gift given that yields great fruit?
“The four who have entered the path and the four who are established in the fruit—
this is the Saṅgha, upright.”
Established in wisdom and virtue,
[he is the refuge] for people who are making offerings,
for living beings who long for merit.
“Merit pertaining to the acquisitions that one performs, Given to the Saṅgha, yields great fruit.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 11.17 (SN 11.17, SN 263, PTS [1st ed. SN i 233, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 501)
2. The Second Chapter:
The Discourse on Paying Homage to the Buddha.
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had retired for his midday rest in seclusion.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati approached the Blessed One; having approached, they each stood leaning against a doorpost.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
Having laid down the burden and being free from debt, wander through the world;
your mind is well-liberated.”
“As when the moon on the fifteenth night.
“It is not, Lord of the Devas, that the Tathāgatas should be venerated in such a way.
And rather, Lord of the Devas, the Tathāgatas should be venerated thus:”
“Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world.
May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma.”
“They will become those who have direct knowledge.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 11.18 (SN 11.18, SN 264, PTS [1st ed. SN i 234, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 502) 2.
Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Discourse on the Homage of Householders.
At Sāvatthī.
There, [the Blessed One] said this:
“Bhikkhus, in the past, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed his charioteer Mātali:
‘Harness, dear Mātali, the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds. Let us go to the pleasure grove to see the beautiful terrain.
‘Very well, venerable sir,’ Mātali the charioteer replied to Sakka, lord of the devas. Having harnessed the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds, he informed Sakka, lord of the devas.”
“‘My dear sir, your thousand-yoked chariot of noble steeds is indeed ready.
Do now as you deem fit,’ he said.
Then, monks, as Sakka, lord of the devas, was descending from the Vejayanta Palace, he joined his palms in reverential salutation and paid homage to the various quarters.”
Then, monks, Mātali the charioteer addressed Sakka, lord of the devas, with a verse:
“The masters of the three Vedas and all the terrestrial kshatriyas pay homage to him.”
The four Great Kings and the glorious Thirty-three—
what name indeed could that yakkha have?
“Whom you worship, Sakka? “The possessors of the threefold knowledge worship me,
as do all the terrestrial kṣatriyas.”
The four Great Kings and the glorious Thirty-three gods, and I myself,
[revere] those endowed with virtue.
I pay homage to those who have long been concentrated in meditation, who have gone forth rightly,
and who are devoted to the holy life.
Those householders who perform meritorious deeds,
virtuous lay followers,
who maintain their wives in accordance with the Dhamma—
“Those I revere, Mātali.
“O Sakka, those whom you revere are indeed the best in the world.”
"I too revere those whom you revere, O Vāsava.
Having said this, Maghavā—
Sujampati, the king of the gods,
having paid homage to the various quarters,
mounted his chariot facing forward.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.19 (SN 11.19, SN 265, PTS [1st ed. SN i 235, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 504) 2. Second Chapter: The Discourse on Paying Homage to the Teacher Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu pays homage to the Teacher, he should pay homage with these three things: ‘The Teacher has abandoned lust; may I too abandon lust. This is the first thing with which a bhikkhu who pays homage to the Teacher should pay homage. ‘The Teacher has abandoned hatred; may I too abandon hatred. This is the second thing with which a bhikkhu who pays homage to the Teacher should pay homage. ‘The Teacher has abandoned delusion; may I too abandon delusion. This is the third thing with which a bhikkhu who pays homage to the Teacher should pay homage. When a bhikkhu pays homage to the Teacher, he should pay homage with these three things. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The Teacher has abandoned lust, The Teacher has abandoned hatred, The Teacher has abandoned delusion; May I too abandon them all. Having paid homage to the Teacher thus, With a mind well-released from lust, A bhikkhu, having severed the fetters, Is one who has gone beyond all suffering.”
At Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
“Bhikkhus, once in the past, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed his charioteer Mātali:
‘Friend Mātali, harness the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds; let us go to the pleasure grove to see the beautiful grounds.’”
“‘So be it, venerable sir,’ Mātali the charioteer replied to Sakka, lord of the devas. Having yoked the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds, he informed Sakka, lord of the devas:
‘My lord, the chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds is yoked.
Now is the time for you to do as you deem fit.’”
Then, monks, as Sakka, lord of the devas, was descending from the Vejayanta Palace, he paid homage to the Blessed One with palms joined.
Then, monks, Mātali the charioteer addressed Sakka, lord of the devas, in verse:
"For that which both devas and humans..."
“Vāsava, they pay homage to him;
who then is that yakkha whom you,
Sakka, pay homage to?”
“He who here in this world with its devas is the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the Teacher of incomparable name— ”
I pay homage to them, Mātali,
for whom lust, hatred,
and ignorance have been faded away.
Those who have destroyed the taints, the Arahants—
those I revere, Mātali,
who have brought about the subduing of passion and hatred.
Through the transcendence of ignorance,
those in training, delighting in the dismantling [of defilements], should train themselves with diligence.
“Those I revere, O Mātali.
“Indeed, those whom you revere, Sakka, are the most excellent in the world;”
"I too revere those whom you revere, O Vāsava.
Having said this, Maghavā—
Sujampati, the king of the gods,
having paid homage to the Blessed One,
mounted his chariot with his face turned toward him.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.20 (SN 11.20, SN 266, PTS [1st ed. SN i 235, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 506) 2.
Second Chapter: Saṅghavandanāsutta (The Discourse on Paying Homage to the Saṅgha)
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
“In the past, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed his charioteer Mātali:”
“Harness, dear Mātali, the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds; let us go to the park grounds to see the beautiful landscape.
“Very well, Blessed One,” the charioteer Mātali replied to Sakka, lord of the devas. Having harnessed the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds, he informed Sakka, lord of the devas:
“My lord, the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds is ready.”
"Do as you deem it timely now.
Then, monks, as Sakka, lord of the devas, was descending from the Vejayanta Palace, he paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with his hands joined in reverential salutation.
Then, monks, Mātali the charioteer addressed Sakka, lord of the devas, in verse:
For these people, lying upon their putrid bodies, would indeed worship him;
they are submerged in a corpse.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst—
why indeed do you envy them,
O Vāsava, those who dwell as homeless ones?
“Tell us the conduct of the seers;
we wish to hear your words.
“I desire this for them,” [he replied].
O Mātali, those who have gone forth from the home life leave the village and depart without looking back.
They do not store [food] in granaries,
nor in jars, nor in baskets;
seeking what has been prepared by others, they live.
By that they subsist, those of good vows,
the wise who delight in the beautiful,
remaining silent as they move through the world.
The gods were at variance with the asuras,
and so were mortals divided among themselves, O Mātali;
yet I remained unopposed amidst those who were opposed.
“Those who have extinguished the rod toward themselves,
who are without grasping among those who grasp—
them I revere, Mātali.”
"Truly, O Sakka, those whom you revere are the best in the world;
I too shall revere them."
"Those whom you revere, Vāsava.
Having said this, Maghavā,
the king of the gods and lord of the Sujās, spoke.
Having paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
he mounted his chariot facing forward.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Its summary verse:
Three deities are mentioned,
as well as poverty and the delightful forest.
The sacrifice, the patron, and the homage—these three are for the sake of honoring the worthy ones.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 11.21* (SN 11.21, SN 267, PTS [1st ed. SN i 237; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 508)
3. The Third Chapter: The Discourse on Having Cut Off.
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“What must one cut off to sleep in happiness?”
"What is it that, when cut off,
one does not grieve? Of what single thing,
O Gotama, do you approve the destruction?"
Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily;
having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
Of anger, which has poison for its root—
“O Vāsava, the Noble Ones praise the cutting off of the sweet tip;
for having cut that off, one does not grieve.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 11.22 The Third Chapter: Ugliness **Dubbaṇṇiya Sutta: On Ugliness** “Monks, there are these five bases for the origination of craving. What five? Visible forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... Odors cognizable by the nose... Tastes cognizable by the tongue... Tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust. These, monks, are the five bases for the origination of craving. When one dwells with a mind obsessed by greed for these five bases for the origination of craving, one does not know or see things as they really are. Not knowing and not seeing things as they really are, one generates desire for them. Having generated desire for them, one becomes infatuated with them. Being infatuated with them, one becomes enslaved by them. Being enslaved by them, one is overcome by them. Overcome by them, one is bound by them. Bound by them, one is called ‘ugly’ (dubbaṇṇa). Why is that? Because, monks, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for ugliness. When one dwells with a mind obsessed by hatred for these five bases for the origination of craving... [and so on] ...one is called ‘ugly. Why is that? Because, monks, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for ugliness. When one dwells with a mind obsessed by delusion regarding these five bases for the origination of craving... one is called ‘ugly. Why is that? Because, monks, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for ugliness. When one dwells with a mind obsessed by greed, hatred, and delusion regarding these five bases for the origination of craving, one does not know or see things as they really are. Not knowing and not seeing things as they really are, one generates desire for them. Having generated desire for them, one becomes infatuated with them. Being infatuated with them, one becomes enslaved by them. Being enslaved by them, one is overcome by them. Overcome by them, one is bound by them. Bound by them, one is called ‘ugly. Why is that? Because, monks, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for ugliness. But when one dwells with a mind free from greed for these five bases for the origination of craving, one knows and sees things as they really are. Knowing and seeing things as they really are, one does not generate desire for them. Not generating desire for them, one is not infatuated with them. Not being infatuated with them, one is not enslaved by them. Not being enslaved by them, one is not overcome by them. Not being overcome by them, one is not bound by them. Not being bound by them, one is called ‘beautiful’ (subhaṇṇa). Why is that? Because, monks, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for beauty.”
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove.
There, the Blessed One... [as before] ...said this:
“Once upon a time, monks, a certain yakkha who was ugly and deformed sat upon the throne of Sakka, the lord of the devas.
Thereupon, monks, the gods of the Thirty-three were indignant, disparaging, and complained, saying:
"It is wonderful indeed, sirs! It is marvelous indeed, sirs!
This ugly, deformed yakkha sits upon the throne of Sakka, lord of the devas!"
“Bhikkhus, the more the gods of the Thirty-three complained, grumbled, and became indignant, the more that yakkha became more handsome, more beautiful, and more pleasing to behold.
Then, bhikkhus, the gods of the Thirty-three approached Sakka, the lord of the devas; having approached, they said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas:
‘Here, dear sir, a certain yakkha—ugly and deformed—is sitting on the seat of Sakka, the lord of the devas.’”
Thereupon, dear sir, the gods of the Thirty-three were indignant, disparaging, and complained, saying:
"It is wonderful indeed, sirs! It is marvelous indeed, sirs!
This ugly, deformed yakkha is sitting on the throne of Sakka, lord of the devas!"
“Mārisa, in whatever way the devas reproach, grumble, and complain, in that very way that yakkha becomes more handsome, more beautiful, and more pleasing to behold.
Surely, Mārisa, that must be a yakkha who feeds on anger.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, approached that yakkha who feeds on anger.

Having approached, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and knelt with his right knee on the ground, he extended his joined palms toward where the yakkha Kodhabhakkha was and announced his name three times:
“I am Sakka, dear sir, lord of the devas; I am Sakka, dear sir, lord of the devas.”
“Monks, in whatever way Sakka, lord of the devas, announced his name, in that very way that yakkha became increasingly more ugly and more deformed.
Having become increasingly more ugly and more deformed, he vanished right there.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, having sat down on his own seat, spoke these verses at that time, exhorting the Tāvatiṃsa devas:”
‘My mind is not easily provoked,
nor am I led astray by your enticements;
I do not become angry with you for long.’
Anger does not abide within me.
When angry, I do not speak harshly,
nor do I disparage the teachings.
“I restrain myself, clearly seeing my own welfare.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 11.23 (SN 11.23, SN 269, PTS [1st ed. SN i 238; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 512)
3. Third Chapter:
The Discourse on the Deceit of Śambara.
At Sāvatthī... [as before]...
The Blessed One said this:
"In the past, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the devas, approached Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, to inquire after his illness."
Bhikkhus, Vepacitti the lord of the asuras saw Sakka the lord of the devas approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to Sakka the lord of the devas:
“Cure me, lord of the devas!”
“Teach me, Vepacitti, the *sambarimāya*,” he said.
“I will not teach it yet, dear sir, until I have consulted with the asuras,” replied Vepacitti.
Then, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, consulted with the asuras:
“‘I shall teach the Sakka, lord of the gods, the *Sambarimāyā*, dear sir,’ he said.
‘Do not, dear sir, teach the Sakka, lord of the gods, the *Sambarimāyā*.
Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, addressed the Sakka, lord of the gods, with a verse:”
“Māyāvī, Maghavā, Sakka,
the king of gods, Sujampati—
he too goes to a terrible hell.”
“Only the restrained among the restrained,” so it was said.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 11.24 (SN 11.24, SN 270, PTS [1st ed. SN i 239, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 513) 3. Third Chapter.
The Discourse on Transgressions.
At Sāvatthī... in a certain monastery.
Now at that time, two monks were engaged in a dispute.
There, a certain bhikkhu committed an offense.
Then that bhikkhu confessed his offense as an offense before the other bhikkhu,
but that bhikkhu did not accept it.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here two bhikkhus were engaged in conversation, and one of them overstepped [the bounds].
Then, venerable sir, that bhikkhu confessed his transgression as a transgression to the other bhikkhu, but that bhikkhu would not accept it.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of fools:
one who does not see his transgression as a transgression, and one who, when another confesses a transgression, does not accept it in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, bhikkhus, are the two kinds of fools.”
“Monks, there are these two wise ones:
he who sees his transgression as a transgression, and he who, when one confesses a transgression, accepts it in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the two wise ones.”
“Bhikkhus, once in the past, Sakka, lord of the devas, while addressing the Tāvatiṃsa devas in the Sudhamma assembly hall, on that occasion recited this verse:
‘Let anger come under your control,

Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Discourse on Non-Anger.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus... [as usual] ...and the Blessed One said this:
“In the past, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, while addressing the Tāvatiṃsa devas in the Sudhamma assembly hall, on that occasion recited this verse:
‘Let not anger overcome you.’”
And do not become angry at those who are angry;
freedom from anger and non-violence are the way of the Noble Ones.
“Then anger crushes the evil person,
just as a mountain crushes [what lies before it].
Thus ends the third chapter.
Its summary verse:
Having cut off ugliness and deceit,
one is free from anger after a transgression.
This indeed is the "Sakka’s Five Questions," taught by the Best of Buddhas.
The Saṃyutta on Sakka is complete.
